🗒️What This Means For You
  • Fed Hike: Since the 2026-09-16 Fed hike the Treasury-rate leg of IG returns is -1.49% (intraday, 7-year +21bp). At trading day 11 (last close) it was -1.25% against a five-campaign average of -0.05% at the same point — 1994-95, 2022-23 were worse. The spread leg adds -0.42%. The 10-year is +25bp since the hike vs a +1bp campaign average at the same point.
  • HY Contagion: Junk-bond stress: the CCC-to-single-B spread gap is 678bp against a five-year average of 408bp (widest since May 2020). Better-rated junk is following: single-B +56bp and BB +47bp in a month. CCC and single-B are moving together more (correlation 0.30 → 0.47 over 3 months; five-year norm 0.70). Investment grade is untouched (+3bp).
  • Stocks: US stocks rose about 0.7%; tech-heavy Nasdaq led, Japan fell almost 1%.
  • FX: The dollar eased slightly; the euro is still below its recent trading range.
  • Technicals: US stocks sit far above their usual range, so a pullback gets likelier.
  • Sectors: Tech keeps leading; banks, utilities and property shares slid for a month.
  • Credit/Spreads: Risk premiums on safer company bonds stay low, but junk-bond premiums are rising.
  • Crisis: Long-term government borrowing costs are high, so pressure on debt-heavy governments is building.
  • Inflation: Underlying inflation is slowly cooling, but a quarter of prices still rise quickly.
  • Tech Bubble: Stocks are expensive and concentrated, but less frenzied than they were in 2000.
  • Earnings & IPOs: PepsiCo is the biggest name reporting; Delta has the biggest expected price swing.
  • Iran: The war continues; oil shipping through Hormuz remains disrupted and oil prices high.
  • Warsh: The Fed chair sounds firm on inflation; a hold is expected at the October meeting.
  • Week Ahead: Next week: Constellation, PepsiCo and Delta report earnings; the CPI inflation report follows a week later.
  • Outlook: Neutral near term; rising junk-bond stress makes the coming months riskier.
  • Trades: Trim stretched Nasdaq positions, hedge junk-bond exposure, buy 10-year Treasuries.
  • Trades Vol: 45 watchlist names screened: 2 buy, 22 hold long, 21 stay out
  • Treasury Liquidity: Treasury liquidity/rates-vol monitor: TLT 95/100 put skew +0.78 vol pts, Fed DKW real term premium +78bp.
  • 10Y Pattern: 10Y at 99th pctile, +1bp from the 2026 rim — still compressing, not a cup-and-handle.
  • Diesel Futures: Diesel: 1-9 of 10 signals point lower.
  • Bottom line: Stock prices look calm while junk-bond stress quietly spreads; keep some protection on.

Friday closed risk-on on the surface. The S&P 500 rose 0.73% to 7722.72, the Nasdaq Composite gained 1.19% to 27190.86, the Russell 2000 added 0.94% and VIX fell 1.08 to 15.31. Europe joined in (Euro Stoxx 50 +1.02%), while the Nikkei lagged at -0.94%. US rates did not rally with stocks. The 2Y rose 3.3bp to 4.8247% and the 10Y rose 3.0bp to 5.2706%, while Bunds (-4.6bp), Gilts (-3.2bp) and JGBs (-3.2bp) all rallied. The US is leading the global bond selloff, and the 10Y sits 18.29% above its 200-day average (computed). The bigger story is in junk bonds, and this week's equity rally does not show it. On Bloomberg's ladder (as of Oct 1), the Caa–B gap is 678bp. That is far above its 5-year average of ~408bp and at the 99.6th percentile of the last 5 years. Caa OAS is 988bp, up 117bp in a month and 210bp in three months. The question is whether the stress is spreading up the ladder, and in the past month it has started to. Single-B OAS widened 56bp in a month to 310bp, BB widened 47bp to 195bp, and the HY–IG gap widened 51bp to 235bp. Investment grade is mostly holding: IG is 83bp, only +3bp on the month, though +6bp on the week. The 63-day Caa/B correlation of daily changes is 0.47. That is up from 0.36 a month ago and 0.30 three months ago, but still below its 5-year median of 0.70. Co-movement is rising but not yet at a full contagion regime. On the FRED cross-check, the ICE CCC OAS is 1215bp, the widest in its 2023-onward sample. This is a descriptive read, not a validated signal. Compared with the prior session, sentiment improved: stocks rallied, vol fell and the dollar eased (DXY -0.17%). Underneath, credit and the long end are tightening financial conditions. The labor panel shows payrolls at 29 (thousand) and unemployment at 4.2%, a soft labor backdrop for a Fed whose chair still sounds hawkish.

“Stocks are celebrating at the top while the junk-bond market is quietly getting worse, so enjoy the rally but don't let go of your hedges.”
📊Markets

US equities finished the week firm. The S&P 500 rose +0.73% (7722.72), the Nasdaq +1.19% (27190.86), the Dow +0.49% (51176.96) and the Russell 2000 +0.94% (2832.895). VIX fell 6.59% to 15.31. In Europe, the Euro Stoxx 50 gained +1.02%, the STOXX 600 +0.75% and the FTSE 100 +0.32%. The Nikkei 225 fell -0.94% to 68309.46. In rates, the US 2Y rose to 4.8247% (+3.3bp), the 10Y to 5.2706% (+3.0bp) and the 30Y to 5.6195% (+0.7bp), which bear-flattened the front of the curve. The Bund 10Y fell to 3.462% (-4.6bp), the Gilt 10Y to 5.366% (-3.2bp) and the JGB 10Y to 3.093% (-3.2bp). In commodities, WTI fell -1.90% to 91.11 while Brent rose +0.41% to 102.73, leaving the Brent–WTI gap wide. Gold fell -0.87% to 4141.19, silver -1.03%, copper rose +0.17% and nat gas +2.29%.

Two-sided analog episodes per signal: days where the signal's percentile-rank (vs its own full history) was <=5th or >=95th, or |z-score|>=1.3, clustered into one episode per zone per >=6-month gap between episode starts. For each zone, the realized forward 6-month % change in the BENCHMARK'S OUTRIGHT PRICE from each episode start is measured; a card's direction (BUY/SELL) is whichever sign that median historical move carries. Entry/target/stretch/stop are computed directly from this table -- the narrative prose (thesis/rationale) is the only part supplied by an LLM, and it is not permitted to alter a number. Crack spreads and curve shapes are, financially, relative-value signals rather than clean predictors of outright price; expressing every card in outright price terms is a deliberate simplification. HO36 Comdty (ULSD's 36-month point) is thin/less liquid on this seat -- treat its curve-shape reading with lower confidence than the others. Not investment advice.

Churn = the longest window of 20-120 sessions whose close range is <= 8x its median ATR(14), with median ADX(14) < 20, an insignificant close-price slope (p > 0.05), and >= 2 entries into each edge zone (top/bottom 20% of the band). Support/resistance = median swing low/high (+/-5 sessions); outer edges = the window's extreme closes. Breakout = a close beyond the outer edge by > 0.5 ATR, confirmed by a second close or one close beyond 1 ATR. A break back inside within 5 sessions is a failed break. An episode's outer edges can widen at most 0.5 ATR past their first detection, so a slow grind can't drag the range along with it. Base rates come from replaying the same rules over the full history, day by day, with no lookahead. This is pattern analysis of historical prices, not investment advice.

🔄Sector Analysis

Growth versus everything else is the dominant theme. US Info Tech is +1.06% today, +7.06% over the month and +30.13% YTD. Global Tech is +6.31% for the month and +37.49% YTD. Over the past month, rate-sensitive and value groups were hit hard. US Financials fell -7.02%, Utilities -6.19%, Real Estate -6.10%, Materials -6.56% and Staples -4.06%. That pattern fits a 5%+ 10Y and junk-credit widening hurting balance-sheet- and funding-sensitive sectors. Energy is the YTD value winner (US +37.49%, global +32.23%) but is -2.55% for the month. Cyclicals bounced today (Cons Discr +1.38%, Materials +1.00%, Industrials +0.78%), but the 1-week and 1-month windows are mostly negative outside Tech and Energy. Defensives are not acting as a haven either: Health Care is -3.75% for the month and Staples -4.06%. In short, leadership is narrow and growth-led, which is fragile if Tech's stretch unwinds.

US HY is at 8% of the 2022 hike peak, and EUR IG and HY are at 15% and 13% of COVID levels. Under the surface, the HY quality ladder is splitting apart. Caa is 988bp (+117bp in a month) and the Caa–B gap is 678bp, at the 99.6th percentile over 5 years. In the past month, B widened +56bp to 310bp and BB +47bp to 195bp. IG moved only +3bp. The Caa/B correlation rose from 0.30 to 0.47 but remains below its 0.70 median. This is descriptive, not a validated signal. Key levels: US HY OAS 375–400bp would require BB/B to keep widening at the past month's pace and IG to break above ~95–100bp, likely triggered by a growth scare (soft payrolls) or an equity drawdown. A retreat to ~290bp would require the Caa stress to stay contained and the B/BB moves to reverse. US IG near 100bp+ is the level at which this would turn from a junk story into a broad credit story.

Widening velocity, not level. Near an all-time high a 63d widening past the trigger has historically raised P(SPX -10% within 3m) from ~8.6% to ~21.9% (Baa p=0.013, HY p=0.028, IG p=0.047, 1990-2026, corroborated on three independently-sourced series). The spread LEVEL carries no such signal once you control for already being in a drawdown (p=0.562) — tight spreads near a high are expected and are not reassurance. ARMED marks elevated tail RISK, not a sell: 78% of past ARMED episodes did not produce a 10% drawdown. 💧Treasury liquidity & rates volcomputed

US Govt Securities Liquidity Index (GVLQUSD), MOVE, Fed DKW term premium and TLT option skew, live from Bloomberg + federalreserve.gov.

Five charts tracking the mechanism Simon White laid out for why Treasury liquidity is deteriorating: rising inflation volatility feeds into a higher term premium, which steepens the curve, which raises bond vol, which shows up as worse UST market liquidity. Right now UST liquidity is at the 48th percentile of its own history (higher = worse) and the Fed's own DKW real term premium is +78bp.

Latest reading is +0.78 vol points (30th percentile of the 33 runs recorded so far). Positive means the 5%-OTM put is pricier than the at-the-money option -- the market paying up for downside-price / higher-yield insurance on long-end Treasuries.

UST liquidity index is 1.51 (48th percentile of its own 2007-present history -- 100th = worst liquidity on record), deteriorating over the past 3 months (+0.05 pts). CPI YoY volatility (2yr) is 0.49pp; the article's thesis is that rising inflation vol drags liquidity worse, which this chart is built to let you check month to month.

Real term premium is +78bp (90th percentile of its own 2007-present history), up 10bp over the trailing ~2 months. Inflation risk premium is +11bp. Fed staff's own DKW decomposition (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei) splits the rise in long yields into a policy-uncertainty component (real term premium) and an inflation-uncertainty component -- both rising is the article's read that this move isn't just a rate-expectations story.

MOVE is 107.3 (78th percentile of its own post-2007 history). The 3m10s curve is 117bp (steeper by 45bp over 3 months). The article's claim is mechanical, not just correlated -- a steeper curve gives forward rates more room to move before converging to spot, which is itself higher realized/implied vol.

MOVE and the UST liquidity index have moved together with a full-history correlation of +0.72 (both series read as 'worse' when they rise). That's the closing link in the article's chain: inflation vol -> term premium -> curve steepness -> bond vol -> liquidity.

Recreates 5 charts from Bloomberg MacroScope, 'Treasury Market Liquidity Is a Live Issue Again' (Simon White, 19-Aug-2026). TLT skew accumulates one point per report run -- Bloomberg's option-surface field is snapshot-only, not retrievable historically via the API. Term premium is the Fed's own DKW model series (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei), pulled directly from federalreserve.gov, not Bloomberg. Not a trading signal -- a liquidity/vol monitor only.

Retracement of the left-rim decline: 76% (needs ≥90% to pass). 10Y level that passes: 6.16% (89bp above today).
Retracement = (right rim − cup base) / (left rim − cup base) = (5.28 − 0.51) / (6.79 − 0.51) = 76%.
Pass level = cup base + 0.90 × (left rim − cup base) = 0.51 + 0.90 × (6.79 − 0.51) = 6.16%.

Same test on each trailing window: cup base = lowest close in the window, left rim = highest close before it, right rim = highest close after it. Cup complete at ≥90% retracement; above 110% the yield has run past the old high (a breakout, not a cup). No cup inside the window when its left rim is not the highest close of the 91 days before it, i.e. yields were already falling into the window. Pass level = cup base + 0.90 × (left rim − cup base).

🗞️Street View — Where the Cycle Is HeadingCURATED · AS OF 2026-10-01

Consensus is a short, shallow campaign: one or two more 25bp hikes, December more likely than October. The debate is whether hiking into an energy shock ends in recession, and the bond market is already doing some of the tightening.

The Fed

  • Sept 16: unanimous 25bp hike to 3.75–4.00%, the first since 2023. Dots: median one more hike in 2026; 16 of 18 see at least one, 4 see two. Inflation not back at 2% until 2029. (CNBC, FedAndMarkets)
  • Warsh's message was distinctly hawkish (inflation 'too high and broad-based'); the Conference Board calls it 'not a one and done'. (Conference Board)
  • Sept 29, Williams (NY Fed): 'no need for urgency'; one more hike 'late this year' may be appropriate; the biggest inflation shocks have passed. (Bloomberg, NY Fed)
  • Sept 30, August PCE came in soft: headline 3.4% (vs 3.7% expected), core 3.0% (vs 3.3%). October odds fell; December still priced. Kashkari: inflation 'still too high'. (CNBC, CNBC (Kashkari))

Market pricing

  • October 28 hike odds vary widely by venue, roughly 35% to 69% (prediction markets highest, CME futures ~58%), mostly measured before the soft PCE print. (PredictionMarketsPicks)
  • About 83% odds of another hike by year-end; futures price ~93bp of tightening over the next 9 meetings, more than the dots. (Forbes)

Bonds and credit

  • 10-year Treasury above 5.25% (Sept 28), the highest since 2007; 30-year ~5.49%. Drivers cited: sticky energy inflation (Iran war), heavy issuance, AI capex demand. Term premium ~1.0–1.4%. (CNBC, CNBC (Warsh's yield problem))
  • AI-related issuers trade ~115bp vs ~78bp for IG overall; high-yield AI supply $40B year to date vs $12B in all of 2025. BNP and Goldman warn the issuance could pressure spreads. (Reuters, Bloomberg (BNP))

The bear case

  • Rosenberg: the Fed has never hiked into an energy shock without a recession, and AI won't save it this time. (TheStreet)
  • Goldman called the case for hiking 'weak' (demand not overheating, energy inflation should fade when the war ends). Oxford Economics: 'The Fed cannot control energy prices'; the risk is a weaker labor market. (CNN)

Read-through: For bonds, the bigger risk is the long end, not the Fed: term premium and supply keeping the 10-year above 5% matter more than one extra 25bp. The recession call is loud but isn't in any sell-side house view yet.

Curated summary of published Fed, market and economist commentary (news and research via the web), not a computed series and not a forecast. Odds differ by venue and move daily.

🔥Is Inflation Persistent?

Persistence score: 50/100 — Inflation is moderately persistent but cooling at the core. Every median, trimmed-mean and sticky measure (2.2–2.7%) is drifting down and sits close to its historical average. Breadth is still uncomfortable: 28.9% of the PCE basket is rising above 5% (13.2% above 10%, 15.7% at 5–10%), driven by flexible and energy-linked prices (Flexible CPI 4.94%). Core PCE at 3.01% remains above target, so the trend is improving but the job is not finished.

Bubble-analog — today's Nasdaq vs the dot-com cycle (two anchors)

WHY TWO START DATES?
Each line is rebased to 100 at a low the tech bull launched from, so elapsed time lines up. Oct-2022 is today's anchor — it was the prior bear-market bottom. Oct-1990 is the dot-com cycle's equivalent (its literal prior bear bottom). But 1990 predates the internet mania by ~4 years, so the second chart re-anchors the dot-com line to the 1994 reset low, just before the surge ignited, for a tighter like-for-like. Today sits very early under the strict 1990 analog, further along under the 1994 surge analog.
━ Anchored at the prior bear-market bottom (Oct-1990)   ━ today's cycle
━ Anchored at the pre-internet reset low (1994)   ━ today's cycle

Valuation marker: today's Nasdaq P/E (39x) ≈ 22% of the ~175x 2000-peak P/E.

IF THIS RHYMES WITH 2000
Nasdaq fell -78.0% peak→trough (2000-03-10 → 2002-10-09, ~31 months); it took ~15 years to reclaim the high.

The current run, anchored at the Oct-2022 low, is at about 247.5 after 48 months. On the 1990-anchored dot-com path, month 48 was ~235.7, and that path did not peak until month 113 at ~1424. In price-path terms we track the mid-1990s, not 1999–2000. The risk today is less a P/E blow-off and more a valuation and concentration problem colliding with tighter money. Top-10 S&P weight is ~35%, CAPE is ~41 and market cap is ~237% of GDP, against a 5.27% 10Y and a hawkish Fed chair. The signposts that would move this closer to 2000 are: IG and Baa spreads starting to widen (credit tightness is already beyond 2000 levels and has room to unwind), PMIs rolling over, and margin debt (+33.7% YoY, 46%) accelerating. The HY ladder is the one already moving.

⚔️Iran War

The newest verified reporting I could find runs through early September 2026. Nothing dated October could be verified, so the details below may be stale. GlobalSecurity's Day 193 update (Sep 8) reports strikes on crude carriers on Sep 5, including M/T Downy, M/T Stark 1 and M/T Kylo, and about 400+ Iranian sites struck since July 7. On Aug 17, a senior Iranian official told Reuters that Tehran had shifted to a 'fully offensive' policy because of deadlocked peace efforts. Iran and Oman agreed a phased framework for a temporary joint navigation corridor and mine-clearing in Hormuz. Iran said it would not consider the strait open until the US lifts its naval blockade, drops oil sanctions and releases frozen assets. Market read: Brent at 102.73 and the wide Brent–WTI gap are consistent with a persistent shipping risk premium.

🏦Fed Chair Warsh
NEAR TERM

Hold at the Oct 27–28 FOMC, which is widely expected (cited), with hawkish language that resists premature easing. The inference rests on his Aug 28 Jackson Hole message that softer inflation prints have not improved the underlying trend.

~1 YEAR

Inferred: a bias toward holding, with a non-trivial chance of a hike if core PCE (3.01%) stalls. Cuts are possible later only if his long-held view that AI-driven productivity is disinflationary shows up in the data, as he argued in a Nov 2025 op-ed. Balance-sheet reduction is likely to stay a priority given his past criticism of a large Fed balance sheet (inference).

Warsh became chair on May 22, 2026 and has deliberately limited forward guidance, preferring that markets react to data rather than to Fed signalling. His Jackson Hole debut leaned hawkish, which matches the US 2Y at 4.82% and the 10Y at 5.27% outpacing global yields. The tension is that before taking office he argued for lower rates on productivity grounds. The October meeting also falls less than a week before the Nov 3 midterms, which raises political scrutiny of any surprise. Flag: the one-year path is my inference from his record, not a stated plan.

Sources: Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh signals tighter policy in debut Jackson Hole address · Key dates that will define Kevin Warsh's opening months as Fed chair · PNC Economics – What to expect from a Warsh-led Fed · Wall Street bets on 2026 rate rise as Kevin Warsh takes charge of the Fed
